subject: Mechanical Engineering
title: Stress and Strain: The Basics
description: A short lesson to help you apply Stress and Strain: The Basics.

hook.text: Pull a rubber band and it stretches. Pull harder and it snaps. Stress is the force. Strain is the stretch.

buildup.text: Stress equals force divided by area. A thin wire under 100 newtons feels more stress than a thick rod under the same load.

discovery.text: Strain is the change in length divided by original length. It has no units — it's a pure ratio of deformation.

twist.text: The same material can feel tension, compression, or shear stress depending on how the force is applied. Direction matters.

climax.text: Engineers use stress and strain to predict if a part will survive its loads. Every bridge and bolt starts with this math.

punchline.text: Force per area. Stretch per length. Two ratios that govern everything.

quiz.question: Why does a thin wire feel more stress than a thick rod under the same force?
options: Thin wires are made from weaker materials than thick rods
Stress is force divided by area — smaller area means higher stress
The force concentrates at the ends of thin wires
